text:
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA

Citation:

Stav v. Stav,

2014 BCSC 188

Date: 20140205

Docket:
S-134601

Registry: Vancouver

Between:

Lilach
Stav

Plaintiff

And

Gil
Stav

Defendant

Before: The Honourable Mr. Justice N. Smith

Reasons for Judgment

Counsel for the Plaintiff

B.J.
Ingram

In person Litigant:

Gil
Stav

Place and Date of Trial/Hearing:

Vancouver,
B.C.

January
22,23, 2014

Place and Date of Judgment:

Vancouver,
B.C.

February
5, 2014

[
1
]

The plaintiff and defendant are former spouses
who were married in Israel in 1995, moved to Canada in 2002 and were divorced
by order of this court in 2011. The plaintiff then obtained a religious divorce
and monetary judgment from a rabbinical court in Israel. She now seeks a
judgment from this court that would recognize and enforce the Israeli judgment.

[
2
]

That judgment was based on a “ketubah,” a form
of religious marriage certificate or marriage agreement that the defendant signed
at the time of the marriage. The plaintiff wants to use that judgment to offset
the substantial costs that have been awarded against her in the British
Columbia matrimonial proceedings.

[
3
]

The defendant applies to dismiss the claim as,
among other things, an abuse of process, while the plaintiff seeks summary
judgment. The issue is whether the judgment awarded by the rabbinical court is
a foreign judgment of the kind that must be recognized and enforced by this
court.

I.

Background

[
4
]

In earlier matrimonial proceedings, the main
issue was whether the present plaintiff would be permitted to move back to
Israel with the three children of the marriage. In August 2011, Gropper J.
found for the plaintiff. The plaintiff then took the children to Israel and the
defendant followed. In April 2012, the Court of Appeal allowed the defendant’s
appeal and ordered return of the children to British Columbia on or as soon as
possible after June 30, 2012 (decision indexed at
2012 BCCA 154
).

[
5
]

The plaintiff did not return the children as
required by the Court of Appeal’s order and the defendant began Family Court
proceedings in Israel to enforce it. The plaintiff asked the Israeli courts
take jurisdiction and allow the children to remain in Israel. The defendant was
ultimately successful in those proceedings and in subsequent appeals. The
Israeli courts found that the courts of this country have exclusive
jurisdiction over custody and other matters relating to the children. Both parties
and the children have been back in British Columbia since November 2012.

[
6
]

In reasons for judgment dated September 19, 2013
(indexed at
2013 BCSC 1725
), I found that the plaintiff had been in contempt of
court from June 30, 2012, when the Court of Appeal order said the children were
to be returned, to November 7, 2012, when they were in fact returned to
Vancouver. (The earlier proceedings here and in Israel are described in greater
detail in that judgment.)

[
7
]

The defendant was awarded costs of the trial and
appeal, which have been assessed at approximately $70,000. He and the
plaintiff’s counsel agree that some further costs, including special costs that
I awarded on the contempt application, remain to be assessed and will likely increase
the amount owed by the plaintiff to approximately $85,000.

II.

The Ketubah Claim

[
8
]

Parallel to and contemporaneous with the family
court proceedings in Israel, the plaintiff commenced divorce proceedings in a
rabbinical court. It is common ground that Israeli law gives rabbinical courts exclusive
jurisdiction over marriage and divorce of Jewish citizens or residents of
Israel. The judges of those courts are orthodox rabbis who apply religious law.
In this case, the rabbinical court found on June 24, 2012, that the previous
Canadian civil divorce did not affect its jurisdiction to consider a divorce
under religious law.

[
9
]

The religious divorce -- called a “get” -- was
granted with consent of the defendant on October 31, 2012. The plaintiff also
claimed that she was owed money pursuant to the ketubah, which the translation
of the rabbinical court’s judgment refers to as a “Jewish marriage
certificate.” That document apparently provided for a payment to the wife of
$139,000 in the event of divorce.

[
10
]

On May 7, 2013, the rabbinical court awarded the
plaintiff 300,000 new Israeli Shekels, which converts to approximately $96,000.
The court said that, in exercising its jurisdiction to reduce the amount from
what was set out in the ketubah, it considered the plaintiff’s stated
willingness to accept an amount sufficient to offset the costs owing to the
defendant in this jurisdiction.

[
11
]

The plaintiff commenced this action to enforce
the judgment on June 19, 2013. The notice of civil claim simply says that she
commenced proceedings in the rabbinical court, that the defendant was served
with the claim, that the court pronounced judgment in her favor and that the
amount remains owing.

[
12
]

The ketubah is written in Hebrew and I was not
provided with a translation. Counsel for the plaintiff says it is neither
necessary nor appropriate for this court to look behind the Israeli court
judgment on which the plaintiff relies. It is agreed that the document provides
for money to be paid to the wife on divorce, but I have no information about
what the payment represents or the basis on which it is calculated. The
plaintiff agreed in a notice to admit that it was a standard form document and
there was no negotiation of its terms.

III.

Recognition of Foreign Judgments

[
13
]

In considering whether to recognize a foreign
judgment, the Court must first determine if the foreign court has a real and
substantial connection to the action or the parties. If that test is satisfied,
defences are generally limited to fraud, denial of natural justice, or public
policy:
Beals v. Saldanha
,
2003 SCC 72
[
Beals
]. The Court in
Beals

added at paras.
41-42
.

The existing defences are narrow in
application. They are the most recognizable situations in which an injustice
may arise but are not exhaustive.

Unusual
situations may arise that might require the creation of a new defence to the
enforcement of a foreign judgment. However, the facts of this case do not
justify speculating on that possibility. Should the evolution of private
international law require the creation of a new defence, the courts will need
to ensure that any new defences continue to be narrow in scope, address
specific facts and raise issues not covered by the existing defences.

[
14
]

I find that the real and substantial connection
test is clearly satisfied in this case. The Israeli rabbinical court was
deciding on the enforceability of a document that had been executed in that
country as part of a marriage taking place there. At the time proceedings were
commenced, both parties were physically present in Israel. Both parties
appeared before the court and made submissions, although the defendant left the
country before proceedings were concluded.

[
15
]

As for the defences, there can be no suggestion
of fraud or a denial of natural justice. The defendant must therefore show
either that enforcement of the order by a Canadian court would be contrary to
public policy or that the circumstances of this case require recognition of a
new defence.

IV.

Public Policy and Religion

[
16
]

The question of public policy turns on the
religious nature of the ketubah. As said above, neither party has seen fit to
provide me with a translation, but the plaintiff did not dispute the
defendant’s assertion that it is a religious document. The defendant’s efforts
to enforce his order for costs have included an examination in aid of
execution, during which the plaintiff defined the ketubah as a marriage
contract or “traditional prenup” that is part of every Jewish marriage.

[
17
]

In its judgment, the rabbinical court referred
to the parties having been married “in accordance with Jewish Law.” The ketubah
was part of the marriage process.

[
18
]

Divorce proceedings in Canada are governed by
the
Divorce Act
, R.S.C. 1985, c. 3 (2nd Supp.), which also deals with child
and spousal support. Other financial issues, in particular division of
property, are dealt with in provincial legislation, such as the
Family Law
Act [FLA]
,
S.B.C. 2011, c. 25
, and its predecessor, the
Family Relations
Act
, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 128 [
FRA
]. The legislation is intended to deal
not only with divorce, but with its financial consequences. It extends the same
rights to all Canadians, independent of whatever religious obligations or
restrictions they may be subject to.

[
19
]

However, the religious nature of an obligation
does not necessarily prevent its being recognized in civil proceedings. In
Bruker
v. Marcovitz
,
2007 SCC 54
, the parties had, during their divorce,
negotiated a Consent to Corollary Relief in which they agreed to also obtain a
Jewish divorce, or get. The husband refused to comply with that agreement.

[
20
]

The Supreme Court of Canada held that the
agreement entered into during divorce proceedings created a civil obligation,
the breach of which resulted in an award of damages. At para. 46, the majority
adopted the following statement from the dissenting judgment in
Morris v.
Morris
(1973),
1973 CanLII 1200 (MB CA)
, 42 D.L.R. (3d) 550 (Man. C.A.):

That the
contract is deeply affected by religious considerations is not determinative of
the issue. That is the beginning and not the end of the matter. Some contracts
rooted in the religion of a particular faith may indeed be contrary to public
policy. Others may not. Our task is to determine whether the rights and
obligations flowing from the marriage contract - specifically, the husband's
obligation to give and the wife's right to receive a Get--are contrary to
public policy.

[
21
]

The majority judgment said it was not ruling on
a matter of religion, but was enforcing a civil contract. At para. 47, the
Court wrote:

The fact that Paragraph
12 of the Consent had religious elements does not thereby immunize it from
judicial scrutiny. We are not dealing with judicial review of doctrinal
religious principles, such as whether a particular
get
is valid. Nor are
we required to speculate on what the rabbinical court would do. The promise by
Mr. Marcovitz to remove the religious barriers to remarriage by providing a
get

was negotiated between two consenting adults, each represented by counsel, as
part of a voluntary exchange of commitments intended to have legally enforceable
consequences. This puts the obligation appropriately under a judicial
microscope.

[
22
]

I was not referred to, nor have I found, a case
in which a Canadian court has specifically considered a monetary claim under a
ketubah, but there are cases dealing with what appears to be a similar practice
in traditional Islamic marriages.

[
23
]

In
Kaddoura v. Hammoud
(1998),
1998 CanLII 14937 (ON CTGD)
, 168 D.L.R.
(4th) 503 (Ont. C.J.) the wife in divorce proceedings claimed money owing as
“Mahr,” a payment required as part of the religious marriage. Rutherford J.
held the obligation was not enforceable:

The Mahr and the extent to which it
obligates a husband to make payment to his wife is essentially and
fundamentally an Islamic religious matter. Because Mahr is a religious matter,
the resolution of any dispute relating to it or the consequences of failing to
honour the obligation are also religious in their content and context. …

In my view, to
determine what the rights and obligations of Sam and Manira are in relation to
the undertaking of Mahr in their Islamic marriage ceremony would necessarily
lead the Court into the "religious thicket", a place that the courts
cannot safely and should not go.

[
24
]

More recent decisions in this court have
established that a religious obligation to pay a sum of money may be recognized
and enforced in some circumstances. In
Amlani v. Hirani
,
2000 BCSC 1653

[
Amlani
], Sinclair Prowse J. found that a religious marriage contract
met the requirements for an enforceable marriage agreement under the
FRA
.

[
25
]

Marriage agreements were governed by s. 61 of
the
FRA
and subject to re-apportionment by the court on the basis of
fairness under s. 65 of the Act:

61  (2) A marriage agreement is an agreement
entered into by a man and a woman before or during their marriage to each other
to take effect on the date of their marriage or on the execution of the
agreement, whichever is later, for

(a) management of
family assets or other property during marriage, or

(b) ownership in,
or division of, family assets or other property during marriage, or on the
making of an order for dissolution of marriage, judicial separation or a
declaration of nullity of marriage.

(3) A marriage agreement, or an amendment or
rescission of a marriage agreement, must be in writing, signed by both spouses,
and witnessed by one or more other persons.

(4) Except as provided in this Part, if a
marriage agreement is made in compliance with subsection (3), the terms
described by subsection (2) (a) and (b) are binding between the spouses whether
or not there is valuable consideration for the marriage agreement.

…

65 (1) If the provisions for division of
property between spouses under section 56, Part 6 or their marriage agreement,
as the case may be, would be unfair having regard to

(a) the duration
of the marriage,

(b) the duration
of the period during which the spouses have lived separate and apart,

(c) the date when
property was acquired or disposed of,

(d) the extent to
which property was acquired by one spouse through inheritance or gift,

(e) the needs of
each spouse to become or remain economically independent and self sufficient,
or

(f) any other
circumstances relating to the acquisition, preservation, maintenance,
improvement or use of property or the capacity or liabilities of a spouse,

the Supreme Court, on application, may order
that the property covered by section 56, Part 6 or the marriage agreement, as
the case may be, be divided into shares fixed by the court.

(Similar provisions are now found in
ss.92-94 of the
FLA
)

[
26
]

Amlani
and other
cases with a similar result were reviewed in
Delvarani v. Delvarani
,

2012 BCSC 162
. On the evidence in that case, Powers J. was not satisfied that the
relevant portion of the religious document had been completed at the time the
husband signed it. He added that, even if it was a valid marriage contract
under the
FRA
, the amount involved made it unfair. At para. 210, he
held:

…I am simply not
prepared to accept that Mr. Delvarani would have agreed to such an amount, nor
would it have been a fair agreement as contemplated by the
FRA
. This is
so particularly in light of the very short marriage and the fact that there is
really no connection whatsoever between the amount of money to be paid, the
length of marriage, the need or dependency of Ms. Javadi, or the ability of Mr.
Delvarani to pay that amount.

[
27
]

A common feature of all those cases is that the
claim under the religious marriage document was raised as part of the family
law proceeding, including the claim for divorce. In this case, the matter that
went to trial before Gropper J. in 2011 was based on a notice of family claim
in which the present plaintiff sought divorce, child and spousal support and
re-apportionment of family assets. There was no reference to a claim under the
ketubah, either in the pleadings or during the trial. The plaintiff also made
no effort to bring the matter before the Israeli court until after the Court of
Appeal judgment.

[
28
]

Although the judgment was concerned primarily
with the mobility issue relating to the children, Gropper J. also dealt briefly
with financial issues. She found that the parties had no assets within British
Columbia to divide (certain real property in Israel was clearly not within the
court’s jurisdiction and was not raised at trial). She declined to make an
order for division of debts and dismissed the plaintiff’s claim for spousal
support.

[
29
]

If the plaintiff had raised the ketubah claim,
it may or may not have been found to be enforceable, depending on the evidence.
The plaintiff would have been required to provide evidence of what the document
actually said and the circumstances under which it was entered into. The
defendant would have had the opportunity to present any contrary evidence.

[
30
]

Gropper J. would have been in a position to decide
whether the ketubah created a purely religious obligation or whether it had
civil consequences. If she found that it met the requirements for a marriage
agreement under the
FRA
, she may have had to consider whether it was
fair, having regard to the factors in s. 65.

[
31
]

That inquiry did not take place and the
necessary factual findings were not made. The plaintiff now seeks to foreclose
that inquiry by asserting the court is bound to recognize a foreign judgment
obtained almost two years later. To do so would, in my view, be contrary to
public policy for two reasons.

[
32
]

It would, first, be contrary to the policy of
the
Divorce Act
and the decided cases that the Court will not enforce
religious obligations unless those obligations are shown to be consistent with
and incorporated into the parties’ legal rights and obligations.

[
33
]

Secondly, giving effect to the foreign judgment
in these circumstances would be contrary to the principle of
res judicata

and particularly the doctrine of cause of action estoppel.

[
34
]

In
Reliable Mortgages Investment Corp v.
Chan
,
2014 BCCA 14
[
Reliable Mortgages
], the Court of Appeal very
recently said at para. 35:

The principle of

res judicata
is founded upon two broad principles of public policy: (1)
the state has an interest that there should be an end to litigation; and (2) no
individual should be tried more than once for the same cause, often stated as
no one should be “twice vexed”:
Angle v. M.N.R
.,
1974 CanLII 168 (SCC)
, [1975] 2 S.C.R. 248.

[
35
]

The form of
res judicata
known as cause of
action estoppel requires parties bring forward all claims and defences with
respect to the cause of action in a proceeding. If they fail to do so, they
will be prevented from raising them in subsequent proceedings. The court in
Reliable

Mortgages

adopted at para.
45
the following statement of Cromwell J.A.
(as he then was) in
Hoque v. Montreal Trust Co.

of Canada
(1997),

1997 NSCA 153 (CanLII)
, 162 N.S.R. (2d) 321, [1997] N.S.J. No. 430 (N.S.C.A.):

My review of these authorities shows that
while there are some very broad statements that all matters which
could

have been raised are barred under the principle of cause of action estoppel,
none of the cases actually demonstrates this broad principle. In each case, the
issue was whether the party
should
have raised the point now asserted in
the second action.

[Emphasis in
original.]

[
36
]

The traditional criteria for cause of action
estoppel were summarized in
Cliffs Over Maple Bay (Re)
,
2011 BCCA 180
at
para.
28
:

1. There must be a
final decision
of
a court of competent jurisdiction in the prior action [the requirement of
“finality”];

2. The parties to the subsequent litigation
must have been parties to or in privy with the parties to the prior action [the
requirement of “mutuality”];

3. The cause of action and the prior action
must not be separate and distinct; and

4. The
basis
of the cause of action
and the subsequent action was argued or
could have been argued in the prior
action if the parties had exercised reasonable diligence
.

[Emphasis in
original]

[
37
]

In my view, all of those requirements are satisfied
here. The family law proceeding that was commenced in this jurisdiction and
went to trial before Gropper J. was intended to resolve all issues, including
financial issues between these parties arising from the divorce, to the extent
such matters were within the jurisdiction of this court. Both parties were
resident in British Columbia at the time of the trial and judgment. The claim
under the ketubah did not involve physical assets outside the jurisdiction. It
was a purely monetary claim allegedly flowing from the marriage and its
breakdown. It was a claim that could and should have been advanced at the time.

[
38
]

Rule 9-5(1) of the
Supreme Court Civil Rules,

B.C. Reg. 168/2009, reads:

At any stage of a proceeding, the court may
order to be struck out or amended the whole or any part of a pleading, petition
or other document on the ground that

(a) it discloses
no reasonable claim or defence, as the case may be,

(b) it is
unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous or vexatious,

(c) it may
prejudice, embarrass or delay the fair trial or hearing of the proceeding, or

(d) it is
otherwise an abuse of the process of the court,

and the court
may pronounce judgment or order the proceeding to be stayed or dismissed and
may order the costs of the application to be paid as special costs.

[
39
]

Where it is plain and obvious that the doctrine
of
res judicata
applies to an action, the action should be struck as an
abuse of process under Rule 9-5(1)(d):
World Wide Treasure Adventures Inc.
v. Trivia Games Inc.
(1996),
1996 CanLII 1428 (BC CA)
, 17 B.C.L.R. (3d) 187 at para.
37
.

[
40
]

I find that it is plain and obvious in this case
and this action must be dismissed with costs.

“N. Smith J.”
